explanation: The vestibulospinal tracts (medial and lateral) end on both alpha and gamma motor neurons of extensor muscles, facilitating antigravity tone and postural stability. The medial vestibulospinal tract descends in the MLF to cervical levels; the lateral vestibulospinal tract descends throughout the spinal cord.
keyConcept: Vestibulospinal tracts: medial (MLF, cervical) and lateral (spinal cord) - facilitate extensor muscle tone for posture.
modelAnswer: Medial and lateral vestibulospinal tracts. These tracts facilitate extensor muscle activity to maintain posture and balance against gravity.

explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract shows somatotopic lamination in the spinal cord with cervical fibers located most medially and sacral fibers most laterally. This arrangement reflects the body map with upper extremity representations medial and lower extremity lateral.
keyConcept: Lateral corticospinal tract lamination: cervical (medial) to sacral (lateral) - inverted somatotopic organization.
modelAnswer: Cervical fibers are medial while sacral fibers are lateral. This medial-to-lateral arrangement from neck to sacrum reflects the body map of the corticospinal tract.

explanation: In the internal capsule, the pyramidal tract fibers are organized with fibers for facial muscles in the genu (knee), upper limb fibers most anterior in the posterior limb, and lower limb fibers most posterior in the posterior limb.
keyConcept: Internal capsule pyramidal tract: genu = face, anterior posterior limb = upper limb, posterior posterior limb = lower limb.
modelAnswer: Fibers for face muscles are in the genu; upper limb area lies most anterior and lower limb area lies most posterior in the posterior limb of internal capsule. This anterior-to-posterior arrangement in the posterior limb represents head-to-toe body map.

explanation: The tectospinal tract forms the dorsal (posterior) tegmental decussation at the inferior colliculus level. The rubrospinal tract forms the ventral (anterior) tegmental decussation at a slightly higher level. These two decussations separate the neck and limb motor control pathways.
keyConcept: Tectospinal: dorsal tegmental decussation. Rubrospinal: ventral tegmental decussation. Both control different body regions.

explanation: The spinal cord is supplied by three arteries: one anterior spinal artery (running in the anterior median fissure) and two posterior spinal arteries (running near the dorsal roots). Segmental arteries (radicular arteries) reinforce these along the cord length.
keyConcept: Spinal cord blood supply: anterior spinal artery (1), posterior spinal arteries (2), segmental (radicular) arteries.
modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery (single, midline), two posterior spinal arteries (lateral), and segmental arteries (multiple, reinforce the longitudinal arteries along the cord length).

explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial part of the medulla (including the pyramid, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus) and the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord (including the anterior and lateral horns and white columns).
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery: medial medulla + anterior 2/3 spinal cord (all motor and sensory pathways except dorsal columns).
modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery. It supplies the pyramid, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla, and the anterior and lateral horns plus anterior and lateral white columns of the spinal cord.

explanation: The posterior spinal arteries (usually two) supply the posterior one-third of the spinal cord, including the dorsal horns and dorsal columns. They run along the posterolateral surfaces near the dorsal nerve roots.
keyConcept: Posterior spinal arteries: posterior 1/3 of spinal cord (dorsal columns and dorsal horns).
modelAnswer: Posterior spinal arteries. They supply the posterior horns and posterior columns of the spinal cord, running along the posterolateral sulcus near the dorsal nerve roots.

explanation: The anterior spinal artery is formed by the union of two arteries, each arising from a vertebral artery. The two branches join at the level of the foramen magnum to form a single median anterior spinal artery that descends in the anterior median fissure.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery: single median artery formed by union of two branches from vertebral arteries.
modelAnswer: It is a single median artery formed by the union of two anterior spinal arteries, each being a branch of the corresponding vertebral artery at the level of the medulla.

explanation: The posterior spinal arteries may arise directly from the vertebral artery or from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). They descend as two channels on the posterior surface of the spinal cord.
keyConcept: Posterior spinal artery: arises from vertebral artery or PICA.
modelAnswer: Vertebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Either directly from the vertebral artery or as a branch of PICA.

explanation: Radicular arteries arise from various sources: vertebral artery, ascending cervical artery, posterior intercostal arteries, and the first lumbar artery. They enter the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramina and reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries.
keyConcept: Radicular arteries: vertebral, ascending cervical, posterior intercostal, 1st lumbar arteries.
modelAnswer: Vertebral artery, ascending cervical artery, posterior intercostal arteries, and first lumbar artery. These segmental arteries enter through intervertebral foramina to supply the spinal cord.

explanation: The spinal cord veins include: one anteromedian vein (in anterior median fissure), one posteromedian vein (on posterior surface), and two each of anterolateral and posterolateral veins running with the nerve roots.
keyConcept: Spinal cord veins: anteromedian, posteromedian, paired anterolateral and posterolateral veins.
modelAnswer: Anteromedian vein (in anterior median fissure), posteromedian vein (on posterior surface), and four lateral veins running along the ventral and dorsal nerve roots on each side.

explanation: Complete transverse section of the spinal cord produces bilateral paralysis below the level of injury. Location determines outcome: above C5 = fatal (respiratory failure); C5-T1 = quadriplegia; below T1 = paraplegia.
keyConcept: Spinal cord transection: above C5 = death; C5-T1 = quadriplegia; below T1 = paraplegia.
modelAnswer: Above C5: death due to respiratory paralysis. Between C5 and T1: quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs). Below T1: paraplegia (paralysis of lower limbs only).

explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection): at lesion level = ipsilateral loss of all sensation + LMNL; below lesion (ipsilateral) = proprioception loss + UMNL; below lesion (contralateral) = pain/temperature loss. This occurs because corticospinal and dorsal columns cross in the brainstem while spinothalamic crosses at spinal level.
keyConcept: Brown-Sequard: at level = IPSI all sensation + LMNL; below IPSI = proprioception + UMNL; below CONTRA = pain/temp.
modelAnswer: At the level of lesion (ipsilateral): loss of all types of sensation and lower motor neuron signs. Below the lesion (ipsilateral): loss of proprioception and upper motor neuron signs. Below the lesion (contralateral): loss of pain and temperature sensations. This dissociated sensory loss is characteristic of hemisection.

explanation: Anterior spinal artery occlusion causes bilateral UMNL paralysis and bilateral loss of pain/temperature below the lesion. Proprioception and fine touch are preserved because the dorsal columns (supplied by posterior spinal arteries) are intact.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery occlusion: bilateral UMNL + loss pain/temp below, WITH preserved proprioception.
modelAnswer: Bilateral upper motor neuron paralysis below the lesion, bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensations below the lesion, with PRESERVATION of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration sense (since dorsal columns are intact).

explanation: The neostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen. Together with the globus pallidus, these form the corpus striatum. The caudate and putamen are separated by the internal capsule but are functionally connected.
keyConcept: Neostriatum: caudate nucleus + putamen. Striatum = neostriatum + paleostriatum (globus pallidus).
modelAnswer: Caudate nucleus and putamen. These are the input nuclei of the basal ganglia, receiving cortical input. They are separated by the internal capsule but functionally linked as the striatum.

explanation: The paleostriatum (globus pallidus) consists of two parts: the internal (medial) segment (GPi) and external (lateral) segment (GPe). GPi is the main output nucleus; GPe is part of the indirect pathway.
keyConcept: Paleostriatum: globus pallidus internal (GPi) + external (GPe). GPi = output; GPe = indirect pathway.
modelAnswer: Globus pallidus external (GPe) and globus pallidus internal (GPi). The external segment is part of the indirect pathway; the internal segment is the main output of the basal ganglia.

explanation: The basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus) are supplied by central branches of the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery. The lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) are the primary supply.
keyConcept: Basal ganglia: supplied by lenticulostriate arteries (branches of MCA) and anterior cerebral artery branches.
modelAnswer: Central branches of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, particularly the lenticulostriate arteries which penetrate the basal ganglia through the anterior perforated substance.

explanation: The basal ganglia drain into veins that empty into the thalamostriate vein (also called terminal vein), which then drains into the internal cerebral veins and ultimately the great cerebral vein (Galen) into the straight sinus.
keyConcept: Basal ganglia venous drainage: thalamostriate vein → internal cerebral veins → great cerebral vein → straight sinus.
modelAnswer: Veins that drain into the thalamostriate vein, which courses through the basal ganglia region and empties into the internal cerebral veins, then to the great cerebral vein of Galen.

explanation: The caudate nucleus follows the lateral ventricle: the head bulges into the anterior horn, the body forms part of the floor of the body of the lateral ventricle, and the tail runs along the roof of the inferior horn before ending in the amygdala.
keyConcept: Caudate nucleus: head = anterior horn floor; body = lateral ventricle floor; tail = inferior horn roof.

explanation: The three functional lobes of the cerebellum are: archicerebellum (vestibulocerebellum - flocculonodular lobe), paleocerebellum (spinocerebellum - vermis and paravermis), and neocerebellum (cerebrocerebellum - lateral hemispheres).
keyConcept: Cerebellar functional lobes: archi (vestibular), paleo (spinal), neo (cerebral).
modelAnswer: Archicerebellum (flocculonodular lobe - vestibular connections), paleocerebellum (vermis and paravermis - spinal connections), and neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres - cerebral cortex connections).

explanation: The archicerebellum consists of the flocculus (paired lateral structures) and nodule (median part of inferior vermis). It is the oldest part of the cerebellum (phylogenetically) and is connected to the vestibular system.
keyConcept: Archicerebellum: flocculus + nodule. Oldest part, vestibular connections, maintains balance.
modelAnswer: The flocculus (paired lateral structures) and nodule (median part of the inferior vermis). These structures form the flocculonodular lobe, which receives primary vestibular input.

explanation: The paleocerebellum consists of the vermis (median zone) and paravermal (intermediate) zones of both cerebellar hemispheres. It receives proprioceptive input from the spinal cord and controls axial and proximal limb movements.
keyConcept: Paleocerebellum: vermis + paravermis. Receives spinal input, controls axial/proximal movement.
modelAnswer: The vermal part and the two paravermal parts of the cerebellar hemisphere. The vermis controls axial muscles; paravermis controls proximal limb muscles. Both receive proprioceptive input from the spinal cord.

explanation: The neocerebellum consists of the lateral parts of the cerebellar hemispheres (the largest part in humans). It receives cortical input via the pontocerebellar pathway and is involved in planning and executing voluntary movements.
keyConcept: Neocerebellum: lateral cerebellar hemispheres. Receives cortical input, plans skilled movements.
modelAnswer: The lateral parts of the cerebellar hemisphere. This is the phylogenetically newest part (neocerebellum), connected to the cerebral cortex via the pontocerebellar pathway, and involved in planning and execution of skilled voluntary movements.

explanation: The four deep cerebellar nuclei (medial to lateral) are: fastigial nucleus (most medial), globose nucleus, emboliform nucleus, and dentate nucleus (most lateral, largest). The dentate nucleus is the main output nucleus, projecting via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Cerebellar nuclei (medial to lateral): fastigial, globose, emboliform, dentate. Dentate = main output.
modelAnswer: Dentate nucleus (largest, most lateral), emboliform nucleus, globose nucleus, and fastigial nucleus (most medial). The dentate nucleus is the main output, while the fastigial nucleus influences vestibular and eye movements.

explanation: The cerebellum is supplied by three paired arteries: superior cerebellar artery (SCA - from basilar), anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA - from basilar), and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA - usually from vertebral).
keyConcept: Cerebellar arteries: SCA (superior), AICA (anterior inferior), PICA (posterior inferior).
modelAnswer: Superior cerebellar artery (branch of basilar artery), anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA - branch of basilar), and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA - usually from vertebral artery).

explanation: The cerebellum is drained by superior cerebellar veins (emptying into the superior petrosal sinus or straight sinus) and inferior cerebellar veins (emptying into the transverse sinus or jugular bulb).
keyConcept: Cerebellar veins: superior (to superior petrosal sinus/straight sinus) and inferior (to transverse sinus/jugular).
modelAnswer: Superior cerebellar veins (drain to superior petrosal sinus or straight sinus) and inferior cerebellar veins (drain to transverse sinus or jugular bulb).

explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle (ICP) carries afferent fibers: posterior spinocerebellar tract, dorsal external arcuate fibers (from accessory cuneate nucleus), ventral external arcuate fibers (from arcuate nucleus), and olivocerebellar fibers (from inferior olivary nucleus).
keyConcept: ICP afferents: posterior spinocerebellar, dorsal/ventral external arcuate, olivocerebellar fibers.
modelAnswer: Posterior spinocerebellar tracts (proprioception from trunk), dorsal external arcuate fibers (from accessory cuneate nucleus - upper limb proprioception), ventral external arcuate fibers (from arcuate nucleus), and olivocerebellar fibers (from inferior olivary nucleus - climbing fibers).

explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle carries efferent fibers: cerebellovestibular fibers (to vestibular nuclei), cerebelloreticular fibers (to reticular formation), and cerebelloolivary fibers (to inferior olivary nucleus). These complete feedback loops.
keyConcept: ICP efferents: cerebellovestibular, cerebelloreticular, cerebelloolivary fibers.
modelAnswer: Cerebellovestibular fibers (to vestibular nuclei), cerebello reticular fibers (to reticular formation), and cerebello olivary fibers (to inferior olivary nucleus). These form feedback pathways from cerebellum to brainstem.

explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) carries only afferent fibers - the corticopontocerebellar fibers. These arise from the cerebral cortex, pass through the basilar pons, and enter the cerebellum as the MCP. There are no efferent fibers in the MCP.
keyConcept: MCP: afferent only. Corticopontocerebellar fibers from cerebral cortex through pons to cerebellum.
modelAnswer: Cortico ponto cerebellar fibers. These arise from the cerebral cortex, synapse in the pontine nuclei, cross to the contralateral side, and enter the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle.

explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP) carries afferent fibers: the anterior spinocerebellar tract (proprioception from lower limb) and the tectocerebellar tract (from superior colliculus for visual reflexes).
keyConcept: SCP afferents: anterior spinocerebellar tract, tectocerebellar tract.
modelAnswer: Anterior spinocerebellar tract (carrying proprioceptive information from the lower limbs and trunk) and tecto-cerebellar tract (carrying visual and auditory information from the superior colliculus).

explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle carries efferent fibers: fastigioreticular fibers (from fastigial nucleus to reticular formation), cerebellorubral fibers (to red nucleus), and dentatothalamic fibers (to thalamus for cortical relay).
keyConcept: SCP efferents: dentatothalamic (main), cerebellorubral, fastigioreticular fibers.
modelAnswer: Fastigio reticular fibers (from fastigial nucleus to reticular formation), cerebello rubral fibers (to red nucleus), and dentato thalamic fibers (to thalamus for relay to motor cortex) plus dentato rubro thalamic fibers.

explanation: The three main external features of the ventral medulla are: the pyramid (corticospinal tracts), olive (inferior olivary nucleus), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (lateral surface). The pyramids are visible as two longitudinal prominences on the anterior surface.
keyConcept: Ventral medulla features: pyramid (motor), olive (olivary nucleus), ICP (lateral).
modelAnswer: Pyramid (containing corticospinal tracts), olive (containing inferior olivary nucleus), and inferior cerebellar peduncle. These are visible on the ventral surface as longitudinal prominences on either side of the anterior median fissure.

explanation: The cranial nerves with nuclei or roots in the medulla are CN IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal). They emerge from the posterolateral sulcus (IX, X, XI) and anterolateral sulcus (XII).
keyConcept: Medullary cranial nerves: CN IX, X, XI (posterolateral sulcus), CN XII (anterolateral sulcus).
modelAnswer: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), vagus nerve (CN X), accessory nerve (CN XI), and hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). They emerge from the posterolateral sulcus (CN IX, X, XI) and anterolateral sulcus (CN XII).

explanation: The ventral surface of the pons shows: the basilar groove (lodging the basilar artery), the middle cerebellar peduncle (lateral), and transverse grooves between bundles of transverse pontine fibers. The pons has two parts: basilar (anterior) and tegmental (posterior).
keyConcept: Ventral pons: basilar groove (basilar artery), MCP laterally, transverse pontine fiber bundles.
modelAnswer: Middle cerebellar peduncle (on each side), basilar artery sulcus (central groove), and transverse grooves between bundles of transverse pontine fibers. These features reflect the pontine structure with its basilar and tegmental portions.

explanation: The cranial nerves present in the pons are CN V (trigeminal - pontine), VI (abducent - pontine), VII (facial - pontomedullary junction), and VIII (vestibulocochlear - pontomedullary junction). The facial and vestibulocochlear emerge at the cerebellopontine angle.
keyConcept: Pontine cranial nerves: CN V, VI, VII, VIII. Trigeminal (lateral pons), abducent ( midline), facial/vestibulocochlear (cerebellopontine angle).
modelAnswer: Trigeminal nerve (CN V), abducent nerve (CN VI), facial nerve (CN VII), and vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). They emerge from the pontine surface: trigeminal laterally, abducent at the midline, and facial/vestibulocochlear at the cerebellopontine angle.
